summary: Zuiei Ito (1942–2020) specialized in Buddhist studies and Indology, earning degrees at Waseda University and the University of Tokyo. He served as a professor of Buddhist studies at Rissho University from 1980 to 2013 and also lectured at other universities.
Zuigan Goto (1879–1965) was a Buddhist and religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo (1903–1906) and under Sokatsu Shaku. He served as president of Hanazono University in 1932.

Zuiho Yamaguchi (1926–2023) specialized in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, studying at the University of Tokyo, EPHE, and under Jacques Bacot and Rolf Alfred Stein. He held posts at CNRS, Toyo Bunko, and was a professor at the University of Tokyo (1970–1986).

Zuiryu Nakamura (1915–1995) worked in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He studied under Susumu Yamaguchi and Kenryu Tsukinowa, and served as a professor of Buddhist studies at Rissho University beginning in 1945.
Zur Mang Khenpo Pema Namgyal studied under Shenphen Nangwa and Pema Wangchok Gyelpo.
pad+ma la studied under Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche and Dudjom Rinpoche.

Édouard Chavannes (1865–1918) was a sinologist and scholar of Buddhist and Iranian/Central Asian studies who studied at ENS and under Marie-Jean-Léon d'Hervey de Saint Denys. He served as a professor at the Collège de France from 1893 to 1918.

Édouard Huber (1879–1914) worked in sinology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at the Sorbonne and under Sylvain Lévi and Johann Baptist Schibenegg, later directing the China and Indochina department at the EFEO from 1901 to 1905.

Émile Benveniste (1902–1976) was a linguist specializing in Iranian/Central Asian studies and Indology, educated at EPHE and under Antoine Meillet and Sylvain Lévi. He was directeur d’études at EPHE (1927–1969) and Chair of Comparative Grammar at Collège de France (1937–1969).
Émile Chartier (1868–1951) was a philosopher who studied at Lycée Pierre-Corneille (~1881–1886) and École Normale Supérieure (~1889–1892).

Émile Chatelain (1851–1933) worked in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1872–1876) and later held a post there from ~1881 to 1925, as well as at the École française de Rome (1876–1877).

Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) worked in religious studies and sociology. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure and under Wilhelm Wundt, later holding posts at the University of Bordeaux (1887–1902) and Sorbonne University (c. 1902–1917).

Émile Senart (1847–1928) was an Indologist and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Munich and Göttingen under Theodor Benfey. He became a professor at the Collège de France and served as president of the Société Asiatique (1908–1928).

Émile-Louis Burnouf (1821–1907) specialized in Indology and linguistics. He studied at ENS and the University of Paris under Jean-Louis and Eugène Burnouf, later serving as professor at Nancy (1854–1867) and director of the École française d'Athènes (1867–1875).
Émilie Aussant works in Indology and linguistics. She studied under Georges-Jean Pinault and held an attested post at Paris Diderot University in 2014.

Étienne Balazs (1905–1963) was a scholar of sinology, history, and archaeology who studied under Otto Franke (1923–1930). He later held posts at the CNRS (1949) and as professor of Chinese economic history at the University of Paris (~1950–1963).

Étienne Lamotte (1903–1983) was a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar who studied under Louis de La Vallée Poussin, Sylvain Lévi, and others. He served as chargé de cours at KU Leuven (1932–1974) and taught at Saint-Louis University, Brussels.

Étienne Marc Quatremère (1782–1857) worked in linguistics, history, archaeology, and Iranian/Central Asian studies. He studied under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy and served as a professor at the Collège de France from 1819 to 1857.

Ñāṇavīra Thera (1920–1965) was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who studied at Magdalene College, Cambridge. He later trained under traditional teachers Pelene Siri Vajiragnana and Nyanatiloka Mahathera, and served in the Royal Artillery and Intelligence Corps.

Ösel Tendzin (1943–1990) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at Fordham University and under Swami Satchidananda and Chögyam Trungpa. He served as executive vice president of Vajradhatu beginning in 1973 and succeeded Trungpa in 1987.
